title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
prompt:
You are given a nested list of integers `nestedList`, where each element is either an integer or a list whose elements may also be integers or other lists (arbitrary nesting depth). Implement an iterator that flattens it, exposing `hasNext()` and `next()`.

Since this test harness calls a single pure function per test case rather than exercising a stateful iterator across many calls, implement `flatten_iterator(nested_list)` that fully flattens `nested_list` into a single flat list of integers, in the same left-to-right, depth-first order the iterator would produce via repeated `next()` calls. Represent nested lists in the input as JSON-style arrays; represent a plain integer as itself.
constraints: The values of the integers in the nested list are in the range [-10^6, 10^6]
Nesting depth is at most a few hundred levels
hints: You need to visit elements left to right, but 'descend fully' into any list you encounter before moving to the next sibling — that's a depth-first order.
A stack works well: push elements in reverse order so the leftmost ends up on top, and whenever you pop a list instead of an integer, push its contents (reversed) back on top.
Alternatively, a straightforward recursive helper that appends integers and recurses into sublists produces the same left-to-right depth-first flattening more simply.

solution.approach: Recursively walk the nested structure: for each element, if it's an integer, append it directly to the result; if it's a list, recurse into it and extend the result with whatever that recursive call flattens. This naturally produces the left-to-right, depth-first order that a real NestedIterator's hasNext()/next() calls would yield, since each sublist is fully exhausted before moving to the next sibling. An equivalent iterative version uses an explicit stack, pushing a list's children in reverse so they pop off in original order.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) where n is the total number of integers across all nesting levels
solution.spaceComplexity: O(d) recursion depth plus O(n) output
